en: Salutations to that Light of Consciousness who shines at the foot of the banyan tree, having commanded Śrī Kauṇḍinya and all the gods, beginning with Vāgīśa, to fulfill their purpose. 1.

Having first studied the *saṃhitā*, one should, while still in youth, study the *pada*, *krama*, *jaṭā*, and *ghana* recitations, as well as the sciences beginning with the *śikṣā*. The *saṃhitā* consists of the euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*) of words occurring within a breath-pause (*ucchvāsa*), up to the end of a section.
That [recitation] is of two kinds, by way of direct order (anuloma) and reverse order (viloma), extending to the end of the words.

Furthermore, the junctions (saṃdhi) of phonemes (varṇa), syllables (akṣara), vowels (svara), and constituent parts (aṅga) are taught separately in due order; these are known as the four types of *saṃhitā*.
Where there is no *saṃhitā* as in the case of individual words (*pada*), if the *prakṛti* (original form) is known to be *saṃhitā*, those seven are recorded as *saṃhitās*.
One should also join the word (*pada*) and the pause (*avagraha*) with what follows.
That which is endowed with its defining characteristics and is explained in due order—

distinguished by the divisions of nominal and verbal endings and so forth— is called a *pada* by the wise; it consists of a vowel that is either homogeneous (*samāna*), elided (*vilaṅghya*), followed by another vowel (*napara*), or followed by a consonant (*tapara*).
It is declared to have eight characteristics: being unblemished, not to be inferred, having an inferred portion, and so forth.
(7) In due order, there is no purpose [in such a work] for one who knows the compounding of words, because of the prior establishment of well-known authorities and established proofs;
nor is there incomplete proof, nor is it a means for proving anything else, nor does it cause the arising or passing away [of doubt], nor is it heard [as authoritative]. (8)
By the reverse of what was previously established through the vision of the scriptures and meditative concentration, because both [theories] lack support,
and because it is accepted by many virtuous ones and heard in the sacred tradition, the sequence that confers honor upon the True One should be followed.
Having pronounced the word as bound in *saṃhitā*, and having spoken the subsequent [word], [one should proceed again].
One should join [the words] with the subsequent one; the sequence should reach the end of the half-verse (ardharca).

Where a word ending in *ā*, ending in an acute accent (*udātta*), or followed by *āṅ* is seen, one should recognize that as a "three-step" (*trikrama*) transition, as in *mo ṣū ṇaḥ* and *ū ṣu ṇaḥ*. 10–11.
Even very great difficulties, when distinguished by sequential approach,
dissolve like darkness at the end of night when pierced by the sun;
having spoken two steps in sequence, one should then speak the second again as the first.
Furthermore, one should speak in sequence; that which is joined together is known as *jaṭā*. [The sequence is:
once the first, twice the second; twice the first, once the subsequent;
twice the third, once the middle, and twice the first, once the subsequent.

Having uttered the *jaṭā* according to the prescribed rule, if one should indeed speak the third [part] as if joined in reverse and direct order, that is known as *ghana*. It consists of two lines, eighteen lines, or is endowed with sixteen lines.

The *ghana* (compact) meter is said to be fourfold, including the thirteen-foot variety. Where two feet consist of identical vowels and consonants, and the third foot likewise consists of identical vowels and consonants, it is a *dvipado ghana* (two-footed compact) arranged in sequence.

Having untied the *jaṭā* (braided arrangement) of the *trikrama*, one should speak the fourth [syllable] from the junction; whether in reverse or in direct order, it is a dense mass of eighteen words.
When that *trikrama* is joined with the preceding word, two [syllables] are like the *jaṭā*, while the remainder is like the *krama*.
Having spoken [the verse] in reverse order, if one should speak it again in the direct (anuloma) order, that is the *ghana* [type], consisting of sixteen words.

In the *ghana*, the first, fifth, sixth, twelfth, and eleventh syllables are said to be the points of junction (*saṃdhi*) in the *saṃhitā* (continuous recitation), while the others are human (*pauruṣa*).

Those high-souled and best of the twice-born who are devoted to the complete recitation (*pārāyaṇa*) of the *padapāṭha* and other such recensions should be known as purifiers of the assembly (*paṅktipāvana*).
That best of the twice-born who performs the complete recitation of the *ghanapāṭha* even once [is likewise pure].
He is indeed Brahmā, he is indeed Viṣṇu, and he is indeed Rudra; of this there is no doubt.
By speaking [this], the sins committed over ten million lifetimes perish in an instant;
by reciting it with faith and devotion, one obtains the fruit of giving thousands of cows.
Those who perform worship for the reciters shall obtain the merit born of that gift;
he who does so attains the abode of Śiva—of this there is no doubt. That best of men who performs worship with faith for those who recite [the text] likewise attains it.
Dwelling in the world of Brahmā, he rejoices together with Brahmā.
(25) For those who read or even listen to this, there shall be full lifespan and all prosperity; and for those who honor the readers, there shall be incomparable sovereignty. (26)

The state of *pragraha* occurs in the case of a matted lock (*jaṭā*) and also when a syllable is followed by a *ghana*; likewise, even when followed by a final vowel, the rules of euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*) are not applied. However, for words containing short vowels, their shortness remains even in *ghana* combinations.
Lengthening occurs in the *anuloma* [forward order], and it should be joined everywhere.

Furthermore, the statement consisting of five words has been explained, and the subsequent [reverse order] should likewise be understood by the wise in every respect as being like the former; however, the other stated [case] regarding the target in that position would not be like the former. 28–29.

The swift one, the bright one, the seven-fold heat; may he again protect the firmament of the divine Viṣṇu. O Agni, may you be rich in cattle for us; may this sacrifice of ours be surrounded by cattle. May there be no deficiency in it; overcome [the obstacles]! 30.
Those [oblations] of yours which are breath, O Agni, and purify yourself; may the sky be your protection, and likewise your life-force, O Agni, lead [us].

In this [fire], there is curd (*dadhi*), and you are the son of Apis; through Agni, the letter *a* arises from breath. 31. O Agni, grant me long life and vigor; protect me, the luminous one, from human afflictions.
You, the purifier, were born as the forest-fire; having come, you attained the state of fire and became the consumer of oblations. 32. Lopa.

These [verses] of his are for this purpose: *suvaryam*, *pramātṛpreddhaḥ*, *yakṣatyā*, *tvam agne samāḥ*, *tvām agne māghavācāyam*, *rapajjāto niṣīdan*, *apred agne asya*, *tvam agne tvalopaḥ* (33), *ukhyeṅgiraḥ*—these are the *kramyā* verses; he causes [the sacrificer] to drink with the *ghanas*.
In cases such as *bhavaty agne 'gne* and so forth, the elision of the vowel *a* is prescribed.

(34) When there is an elision of *u* preceded by an acute accent (*udātta*) before words beginning with *va* and others, it is stated that the substitution of *ṇ* for the letter *n* following an *ṛ*-vowel would then apply. (35)
The substitution of *va* for the impermanent *ū* has been taught by the rule of the "indicatory short vowel" (*hrasvopalakṣaṇanyāya*) throughout all *ghan* and *saṃdhi* contexts; thus,
the *s* does not undergo the change to *ṣ* here in the phrase "mahi sṛjyadhvam."

That which is preceded by the vowel *ṛ* or the consonant *r* is said to be stronger. In reverse order, the third [consonant] is not [retained]; *na* becomes *nya*, and *ka* does not attain *ṇa*; it attains the third [consonant] of its own class (*prakṛti*) only when followed by *na*. (36–37)
The *s* substitution for the *visarga* in the word *punaḥ* occurs when followed by [a vowel], but in the case of *kṛdhi viśvataḥ kṣatram*, the *visarga* would not be affected; likewise,
the *visarga* in *iḍaḥ* remains when followed by the term *paridhi*.
In that context, one should obtain the letter *sa* preceded by a strong consonant;
the letter *ma* may be either alone as an anusvāra, or followed by *ja*, *gha*, or *na*.
Devoid of any other attribute, it is proclaimed to have two morae (*dvimātra*).
Even a statement such as "api akāra" (even the letter 'a') would partake in the function within the *prakṛti*;
however, in all contrary cases, it would never partake in the function.
If the letters *ya* and *ra* should occur for a given *na*, that [substitution] occurs in its *pauruṣa* form within the *prakṛti*.
That which is prohibited in the original form shall indeed occur when it is reversed.

From that ten-thousandth word, which is not mixed with other vowels, the addition of the letter *vā* is declared here for the *jaṭā* and other such arrangements; this is called the "supreme" (*para*). 42–43.

It is traditionally taught that for the letter *cha* preceded by a vowel, there may be an augment (*āgama*) before it; however, from the letter *ha*, the letters *ṇa*, *ṇa*, *ma*, and *ū* follow, while here [the augment] spreads forward.
When preceded by an *a*-vowel, it attains the state of *e*; when followed by an *i*-vowel, it attains the state of *ai*.

If the *u* sound (*u-ddokāra*) is not followed by *ma*, *e*, *va*, *mo*, or *da*, then it indeed attains the *ai* sound when followed by *a*. Likewise, the *ṛ* sound, when preceded by *a* and situated above [the vowel], attains the *vi* sound. 45–46.

If the preceding vowel is *opaprāvacan* (low-pitched) and the following is *āramṛt* (high-pitched), and if there is an acute accent (*udātta*) in their junction, it is called an *udātta-sandhi*. Furthermore,
a *svāra-sandhi* should be understood as occurring between a permanently acute (*nitya-svāra*) and an unaccented (*anudātta*) vowel.

If there is the mention of "two-footed" (dvipada) regarding either the *nimitta* (the cause/preceding condition) or the *lakṣya* (the target/the following element), [the doubling] should occur by one [letter] in the regular order (*krama*) and by two in the reverse order (*viloma*).
When the letter *la*, preceded by *ṭa*, and the letter *ṭa* itself occur as a *saṃdhi* between those two, [the doubling applies]. 48–49.
In the case of *jaṭā* and other such combinations, both [the preceding and following vowels] likewise attain the state of being double (*dvitva*) and long (*pluta*).
Similarly, when the *i*-vowels and *u*-vowels are acute (*udātta*), they become *ya* and *va* respectively.
If the subsequent vowel is grave (*anudātta*), it becomes a circumflex (*svarita*); this is called the *svāra-kṣaipra*.

That [vowel] which stands in the middle of an uninterrupted word (*akhaṇḍapada*) and is joined with *y* or *v* is called *svarita*. Whether it is preceded by a non-low (*apūrva*) vowel or a low (*nīca*) vowel, it is always declared to be *svarita*. However, when it occurs within various words (*nānāpada*) and is struck (i.e., followed) by a high (*udātta*) vowel and so forth, it becomes *nihata-svarita*.

This is declared to be the *pratihata*; however, it is not that which follows a *svarita* [accent], but rather that which is said to be mixed with an *anudātta* (unaccented) vowel *a*. When an *eṅ* or *kit* [element] occurs before an *it* [element], it is pronounced with the *svarita* accent; that is known by the wise as the *abhinihita-svara*.

When the vowel *u* follows a high-pitched (*udātta*) syllable, it becomes low-pitched (*anudātta*). This [combination] resulting from the junction of both is called the *praśliṣṭa-svarita* by the wise.
In the case of *vivṛtti* (separation), when a word-final high-pitched syllable is followed by another, it becomes a *svāra*.
That which occurs at the end of a word (pādavṛtta) should be understood as such, provided it is not followed by an acute (udātta) or circumflex (svarita) vowel;

if a low-pitched (nīca) vowel follows an acute vowel within a word, it would attain the circumflex accent. This very [circumflex] is called *tairovyañjana*, provided it is not followed by an acute or circumflex vowel.

When the vowels *i* and *u* become *y* and *v* respectively under certain conditions, one should know that this is always the characteristic of the *kṣaipra* [svarita] when followed by an unaccented (*anudātta*) vowel. When a circumflex (*svāra*) vowel is followed by another circumflex, there is another low-pitched (*nīca*) sound of the duration of a mere atom (*aṇumātraka*).
The former [consonants] are known as *kampa* (trembling) if short, while that which becomes long is [the *vikampita*].
Sixteen vowels are to be known; there are twenty-five *sparśas* (stops); four *antasthās* (semivowels), and six *ūṣmans* (sibilants) are proclaimed. 59.

Two *anusvāras*, the *visarga*, the *la*, the *svarabhakti*, and the four *yamas*—thus it is stated in the Yājuṣa doctrine that the number of phonemes (*varṇas*) is sixty; however, according to that view, the *anusvāra* follows a vowel, and a consonant [is followed by another] when a consonant follows. 60–61.
It is held that doubling occurs after a *repha* preceded by a vowel, as well as after the two *lava*s; thus, there is a fourfold possibility regarding this application.
However, among the second and fourth [consonants], there is no doubling within the scope of that application.
Therefore, the prior arrival [of the vowel] should first be understood in the case of the vowels *cha*, *kha*, *bhu*, and *ja*.

Whatever [vowel] is between two consonants with identical vowels—even if it is a prior arrival—it is not explicitly prescribed here because it is already clear through its pronunciation and so forth. (63–64)

When a voiceless sibilant (*ūṣman*) is followed by a stop (*sparśa*), there is an augment (*āgama*) consisting of the first stop of the same place of articulation (*sthāna*) as that [sibilant] inserted between them, and it does not separate those two.
For a stop at the end of a word, and for any other initial stop, there is the doubling of the second [stop].
When *ś* follows, doubling occurs for *r* and *s* that are not at the end of a word; however,
doubling does not occur for *r* or *visarga* when followed by a consonant standing at the end of a pause (*avasāna*), nor in certain instances when followed by the *jihvāmūlīya* or the *upadhmānīya*.

A letter is not doubled when followed by a vowel, nor when followed by a non-initial sibilant (*ūṣman*), nor by a letter of the same class (*sarūpa*) or a letter belonging to the same group (*savargīya*). This prohibition does not apply when a sibilant follows an *uttama* (nasal) consonant; in such cases, the *yama* of the preceding non-*uttama* contact consonant (*sparśa*) is doubled.

Anusvāra does not undergo doubling before a consonant followed by a vowel (69). It does not double before a stop (sparśa), nor does the *l* of *la* or *va* double, nor does it double before *ha* or *sa* when the following vowel is unaccented (*asvarita*) (70).
Furthermore, this applies to nasalized (*ānunāsikya*) syllables at the ends of words (*padānta*) as well as in the euphonic combination of words (*padasaṃhitā*).
One understands that both the original (*prākṛta*) and the modified (*vaikṛta*) forms possess those properties with ease.

When there is nasalization (*anunāsikya*) within a syllable, the best [substitute] occurs before a stop (*sparśa*). If it occurs before a semivowel (*antasthā*), the determination is that it is that very same semivowel. (71)
When a sibilant follows, the *svarabhakti* (vowel-fragment) occurs before the *r* and *l*;

however, it does not occur before a doubled consonant, nor before an *abhinidhāna*, nor when another [consonant] follows that is not the first of the four [classes], provided the last [consonant] follows in sequence. 72–73.
The first [vowels] and so forth are nasalized; likewise, the letter *ś* alone after the letter *h* is nasalized.

Beyond the *prākṛti*, no nasalized [consonant] exists. If, in the case of the *abhinidhāna* of *ś*, *ṣ*, *s*, or *s*, there follows a semi-vowel (*antastha*) or a sibilant (*uttama*) in succession, [the rule applies].

Where the two *la*s are joined together and possess the *nīca*, *ucca*, and *svarita* accents (75), there alone does the doubling occur for the *yoga* and so forth; however, this is not the case when an *ai* or *o* precedes or an *v* follows.
For a *la* that is not joined [to another], the state of having two feet (*dvipādatva*) always occurs (76).
In the words *dhūṅkṣṇāt*, *aṅkṣṇāt*, *ucchansī*, *ghnantṛkṣu*, and *vailvaḥ* as well,
there would be an excess of the nasal (*ṅ*) due to specific rules,
if a word-final *ṅ* preceded by a vowel were followed by the letter *y*. (77)
This twofold form is the consensus of all the sages.

(78) A *ṅ* at the end of a word does not undergo doubling when followed by a vowelless consonant (*avyañjana*). Likewise, an *m* at the end of a word preceded by a vowel (*ac*) does not double when followed by *h* that is not followed by a vowel (*anṛkārapara*). (79)

When the letter *va* is followed by a consonant other than *ra*, preceded by a long vowel, [the *anusvāra*] becomes *ṅa* or *ṇa*; likewise, when it is preceded by a vowel and followed by *ya*, it remains as such at the end of a word. This is called *vatsānusṛti*, as well as *vatsānusāriṇī*.
The Vaiśeṣikā, the Pākavatī, the Madhyā, and then the Pipīlikā;
likewise the Savarṇadīrghī and that which is known as the Ubhayadīrghī—these are the eight designations according to the divisions of the *vivṛtti* vowels. 81–82.

That articulation which has a short vowel as its predecessor and likewise has a long vowel as its successor is called *vatsānusṛti*; it is also designated as *mātrā* and *kāla*. That articulation which follows a short vowel and precedes a protracted (*pluta*) or long (*dīrgha*) vowel [is likewise so defined].
This [metre] is called Vatsānusāriṇī when it consists of a single [foot] joined [with another];
provided that its first and last syllables are long, while the middle syllable is either a dissimilar vowel or the absence of a visarga. (84–85)
That indeed would be a *vaiśeṣikā* [meter], consisting of exactly one *mātrā*; likewise,
if there should be a short syllable both before and after it,
then it is a *pādona-mātrikā*, for that is known as *pākavatī*.
That [vowel] which possesses both long and short forms in its two places,

and where there is a *visarga* and a *svāra* in the euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*), with a *mātrā* situated in the middle— there, according to the characteristics of the "middle" (*madhyaga*), the *visarga* would not occur. 87–88.
That metrical foot consisting of a single mātrā is to be known as *pipīlikā*, provided there is a long vowel by *savarṇadīrgha* at the beginning and a visarga at the end;
however, if there is a *svarita* accent in the sandhi, it is not a single mātrā due to the *savarṇadīrgha*. 89.
If there is no *visarga* there, it is a long vowel of two morae (*mātrā*).
An *anusvāra* is doubled; likewise, the fifth letter of the class following a final consonant is also doubled and possesses two morae.
However, when following a short vowel, it has one mora, and when following a long or protracted (*pluta*) vowel, it is alone [without doubling].
The word *hari* followed by the *visarga* is desired before the *praṇava*;
however, there is no *saṃdhi* for the *visarga* when the word *hari* follows the *praṇava*. It may be used alone, joined with a vowel, or likewise accompanied by a *mātrikā*.
The body, the essence of color, and the five sequences of colors are thus remembered.

(93) One who knows the characteristics is the best; one who knows the object characterized is middling; but he who knows both the object characterized and its characteristics—that indeed is the food which is praised. (94)
A wise person should not abandon the defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*); otherwise, the tradition (*saṃpradāya*) would be corrupted.
Without the defining characteristics, the disciple lacks the tradition and is subject to ruin.
One who does not know the correct recitation does not attain the fruit of that [tradition]. 95.

Without auspicious marks, even pure complexions do not attain purification (96). A woman endowed with beauty is like the wife of a poor man; likewise, speech is like that which lacks melody, and women are like those who lack clothing (97).
In this way, the castes do not shine when they are devoid of life-force, just as embodied beings do not shine without breath.
He who does not know the characteristics (lakṣaṇa) shall not partake of the fruit;
for he who knows the characteristics of Brahmins enjoys every auspiciousness. 98.
Through service to the teacher, through yoga, through austerity, through attending upon the wise,
through discerning exposition, and through time— by these six means one attains knowledge.
Thus ends the Śrī Kauṇḍinya-Śikṣā.
The Kauṇḍinya-śikṣā of Kaundinya: one should know that in some places it is in a single tone (ekaśruti), and in others the prescribed accentuation (svara) is applied.
The *svarabhakti* is independent, yet otherwise it is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the consonant.
Whether it be another vowel or another phoneme, it is observed in five types of questions;
it is prescribed thus at the beginning of two [words] and at the end of three, starting from the *Āraṇya* section.
One should not transgress what is prescribed by the rules, nor should one utter that which is indistinct;
one should not speak that which is overly distinct—this triad is declared by the wise.
Thus it may sometimes be in the Veda, and the same applies to those who follow its practice.
They say that when [the vowel] is always of the same color (savarṇā), it is called the single *śruti*.
The five *svarabhaktis* are to be known as *kareṇu*, *karviṇī*, *hariṇī*, *hāritā*, and *haṃsapadā*. 4–5.

One should recognize *kareṇu* when there are *ra* and *ha*; *karviṇī* when there are *la*, *ha*, *ka*, and *ra*; *hariṇī* when there are *ra*, *śa*, and *sa*; and *hāritā* when there are *la*, *śa*, *ka*, and *ra*. That which consists of *haṃsapada* [units] occurs when there are *repha* (the letter *ra*) and *ṣakāra* (the letter *ṣa*).
The letter *ṛ* should have a duration of three *mātrās*, while the letter *ṝ* has half a *mātrā*.
The letter *lṛ* consists of one *mātrā*, and by means of the letter *lṝ* it is repeated again and again.
*Hariṇī* should consist of one and a half *mātrās*, and *Hāritā* is two *padas* longer.

The *haṃsapadā* consists of three morae (*mātrā*), or it may have an excess of morae; when a short vowel follows a long one in a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*), rapidity is prescribed. Its measure is one mora, or there is a pause in the case of hiatuses (*vivṛtti*).
When the *Śikṣā* and the *Prātiśākhya* are in conflict,
they say that at such a time the *Śikṣā* is extremely weak, just as a deer is to a lion.
If a consonant is seen between two labial vowels, [the rule of the *Śikṣā* prevails].

However, a separation must be made if that consonant is not single; likewise, whether there is a hiatus, a pause, a *svarabhakti*, or even an *anusvāra* is observed, the previously stated rule applies here without doubt. 12.

If many [consonants] are seen between those two, they should be placed separately; however, the superior [consonant] should be applied for the benefit of the inferior one, as well as in the case of labial vowels and when two letters are involved in the operation. 13–14.
In no case should the doubling of the two labial [consonants] occur;
however, if they are seen between two labial vowels,
there shall be no separation between them, but rather a hiatus (*tṛṭi*) of one *mātrā* between the two.
Where the letter *pa* is seen between two labial vowels, there is no separation [of the consonant from the preceding vowel] if the two vowels are of different forms;
however, if the same class-consonants (*savarga*) occur at the beginning and end, that effort [of separation] is desired there. (16–17)

That should be known as occurring at the end [of a word], provided it is likewise in a *saṃhitā* context; where an ending in long *ā*, an acute accent (*udātta*), or followed by the particle *āṅ* is seen,
one should recognize that as a *trikrama* (three-step transition), as in *moṣūṇaḥ* and *ūṣuṇaḥ*.
If a word ending in the letter *na* is followed by the letter *ha*,
and there is no other phoneme between the two *ha*s that is uncombined (*asaṃyuta*),
then, if there is a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*) with the letter *pa* following the *na*, it is circumflex (*svarita*). 19–20.
Then it would indeed be conjoined; otherwise, it would be unconjoined.

A *anusvāra* is one *mātrā* plus two *mātrās*, but from those two *mātrās* it becomes exactly one *mātrā*. Even when followed by a consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*), that which consists of one *mātrā* remains as one *mātrā*, like the form *dvirūpa*.
The duration of the anusvāra is indeed equal to that of a single mātrā in saṃhitā. However, when it occurs in the middle of a word and possesses two forms,
one mātrā is specifically prescribed for the duration of the nasalized sound.
In the *saṃhitā* [recitation], that [vowel] remains as it is, but at the time of the *pada* [recitation], it becomes longer;

from a long vowel (*dīrgha*) or a protracted vowel (*pluta*), there should be one or two morae (*mātrā*) respectively. This is the distinction in the final position (*avasāna*) which does not exist for others.
Therefore, in the Kaṭha [recension], that which was obtained as being separated from the sound is not obtained;
however, in the Taittirīya, the division of the *phala* (result) is recited, and there the prohibition regarding a conjunction with a sibilant (*ūṣman*) is not accepted. 25–26.
By injunction, devotion itself shall be established; the status of being a preliminary limb (pūrvāṅga) is prescribed.
The *ṛ*-vowel and the *ḷ*-vowel are designated as "conjoined" (*pṛkta*); this should be understood in the recitation of the Veda, provided they are related to the Veda and not otherwise. (27)
The vowel arising from the heart is known to have a resonance like the sound of a bronze bell (kāṃsya).

It may possess two or three morae (mātrās) and be accompanied by nasality; it is joined with the final letters of the consonant classes, along with ś, ṣ, and s, as well as the semi-vowels (antasthā). 28–29.
Upon seeing [these], the Yamas turn back; it is said that desire is extremely subtle, as are anger and evil—these three are truly present in the first three [syllables].
One should recognize the *svarabhakti* as the letter *i*; of this there is no doubt.
When a semi-vowel (*antasthā*) or the like arises, the preceding [consonant] is doubled, but the fifth [nasal] is not;
however, when *pada* begins with another [consonant], that [doubling] does not occur—so it is remembered by the wise.
This applies likewise to the *svarita* and *udātta* accents, as well as to those [vowels] joined with a *svarita*. (31–32)
Due to the accumulation of the unaccented [vowels], their function is now described:
first, there is a stronger breath for the word itself, while for the following [consonant], there should be a weaker breath, to be applied according to the sequence. 33.

If the fifth [syllable] follows the fourth at the beginning of a difficulty, it should be known as its repetition; however, if it occurs earlier, it is the third. For one who recites with the left hand, that [recitation] becomes fruitless. 34–35.
That [anusvāra] should be placed after the consonant, and likewise its color;
however, the doubling of the letter *a* in those two cases is not desired everywhere. There is an option for vowels (*acaḥ*) when preceded by a consonant (*tyam*), and that alone.

Wherever a *nakāra* preceded by a *repha* (r) is seen at the end of a word, one should know that there is a specific rule: doubling is indeed prescribed for both the first and the second [consonant], provided it is not followed by a *ṣakāra*. 37–38.
There is a practice to be understood: first, at the very beginning, having transcended the seven notes (*svara*), it sometimes occurs as a circumflex (*svarita*).
Its breath-force (*vāyu*) is slight, and it is traditionally known as "foot-movement" (*pādavṛtti*). (39)

There is a distinction regarding the letter *ṭa*; if the letter *dha* is seen [in its place], it should be understood as a lack of practice (*anabhyāsa*), for there is no doubt that the letter *dha* is not intended here. For the Taittirīyas, the reading accepted in their own traditional recension (*ārṣa*) is as follows: 40–41.
One should recite the first two words of each section (*anuvāka*) at the beginning of that section;
one should not recite from one question to the next unless they are connected by a causal relationship (42). And likewise, one should recite the section without skipping over it.

Those [mantras] which are counted among the words, sentences, and internal sections of the Taittirīya Veda should be employed; by that means, they attain the goal. In the Kaṭhaka, however, it should be known that there are two types of words, and no third category exists.
Whether it be this or that, there is especially a distinction regarding the wording [of the Veda],
just as in the case of those related to the Veda who have excluded the Vedic recitation (vedapāṭha).
Therefore, they always abandon the udātta and other accents due to their connection with the Veda.
The wise declare that what is unaccented at the end [of a word] becomes accented [in sandhi].
Just as it is observed in cases such as *āraṇyā* (at the beginning) and at the end of two [words], so it is exactly like that.
For indeed, [the rule regarding] sound and so forth is intended to apply only among the deities during the sacrifice. 46–47.
They do not perform the work of euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*); that *saṃhitā* belongs only to you.

However, the vowels are to be known as Brāhmaṇas, and those which are the first, second, and third of the consonant classes (*varga*) are Kṣatriyas. (48) And the fourth [consonants] are likewise Kṣatriyas.
The Vaiśyas are the best among the classes, as are the semivowels (antasthā).
The anusvāra, the visarga, and the sibilants (ūṣman) are the Śūdras. How then can the classes of letters—Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and so forth—be [distinguished] among the letters? 49–50.
Because it is their own time, it is said that for Brāhmaṇas it lasts for a full [period],
while for Kṣatriyas and others it is half of that, according to the perspective of the scriptures.
Some, however, declare that for all [castes] it is a quarter, as measured by the understanding of the *mātrās*.
And because of the word "clothing" (vāsaḥ), it is traditionally held that the nasalized vowel (*nāsikya*) at the beginning is not obtained;
alternatively, the *svarabhakti* is proclaimed as independent in the Kaṭhaka, the Pitṛmedha, the Svādhyāya, and the Nārāyaṇa Upaniṣad. 52–53.

This is not so; rather, it is specifically the substitution of *n* for the *ś* in the case of a "badly articulated" (*duḥspṛṣṭa*) initial sound when followed by a conjunct containing *n*. This will be explained later.
However, in the Taittirīya recension, it is taught that the vowel *i* occurs in its place.
In that section, within the first introductory chapter, the rule is as follows:
there is elision of the vowel *u* between the two *su* suffixes, while the preceding accent is tremulous;
there should be a hiatus for the following [syllable], and an insertion occurs between the two feet. 55–56.
One should understand that the letter *ca* is proclaimed there in the *Kāṭhaka*;
if it is described by the learned as being distinguished by that sound,
one should omit the *utkārya*, and its *svarita* nature will certainly remain.

They teach three modes of recitation for speech: slow, medium, and fast. (58) Regarding these different modes, they say there is a distinction in the ritual action; one attains mastery through the distinction of the *mātrā* (syllabic measure).
For the purpose of practice, one uses the fast mode, but for the purpose of formal performance, one uses the medium mode. (59)
For the sake of instructing disciples, one should employ a slow (vilambita) tempo;
in teaching, there is a three-mora duration for each chapter, and its constituent morae are combined. Or rather, the sages state that all three tempos are used in actual performance.
A cat might distress its own offspring with its mouth or with darbha grass;
one should speak of such a "cat-like" sacrificial offering (varṇavali) as being the cause of that [defect].
Likewise, one who sings, one who is too fast, one who shakes his head, and one who merely recites from a written text [are also defective].
One who lacks understanding of the meaning, one with a weak voice—these six are the lowest among reciters.

At the end [of a word], the retroflex consonants (tavargīya) occur; the first and last [consonants of each class] are produced at the root of the teeth. However, a *nakāra* that is not at the end of a word is excluded when it occurs in conjunction (*saṃyoga*).
In the case of *avagraha*, however, the letter *na* is declared to be of two kinds:
it may be at the tip of the tongue or in the middle of the tongue; furthermore, the *na* [is distinguished] by the word "and" (*śca*) and especially by the word "again" (*punaḥ*). 64–65.
Those two [consonants] should be at the very tip of the tongue; likewise, others do not [occur] due to the absence of a vowel.
A doubling never occurs before the letter *r* or the letter *h*, nor before the second letters of a class, nor before the fourth letters of a class under any circumstances. (66)

With the third [syllable], one should suppress the first of the fourth [pāda], and not that of another; the first and the middle of that [fourth] should be pressed by its own vowel alone. At the pause, there should be a single tone, whether acute (udātta) or circumflex (svarita). 67–68.
Whether it be the *prakṛti* or the *saṃhitā*, everything shall be pronounced with a single tone (*ekaśruti*).
However, the letter *k* remains nasalized (*anunāsika*) in the middle, while the letter *g* applies respectively to the letters *t* and *dh*. 69.
One should not emit the breath through the nostrils during the conjunction with *ha* or *ma*.
In the case of *na*, *nā*, *da*, *d*, *u*, *ṛ*, *a*, *sāntya*, as well as in *ya*, *ra*, *la*, and *va*, there is a slight resonance (*īṣannāda*).
For *yaṇ* and *jaś* sounds, it is otherwise, as is the case for the *vṛhat* [svarita] tone. 70–71.
Some desire the syllable *ha*; likewise, there may be a twofold nature [of the mantra].
Merely by reciting the Veda, one becomes free from evil deeds;
like a tuft of cotton cast [into fire], the heap of sins is destroyed.
Brahmins who know the Vedas do not study all the scriptures;
they are certainly like women adorned with every ornament yet remaining naked.
A pause (*virāma*) in the *Ṛgveda* should consist of three morae (*trimātra*), and it should be the same even at the end of a half-verse (*ardharca*).
At the time of a word-break, it should be two morae; in hiatuses, one mora;
in the middle of a word, it should be half a mora—or perhaps three morae at that time. Some say it is three morae, or there may be an excess of length.
In the *praṇava*, there should be three measures (*mātra*); the protracted (*pluta*) should consist of four measures.
They say that the long (*dīrgha*) consists of two measures, while that which is designated as short (*hrasva*) is the duration for which the eyes of a healthy man sitting at ease blink. (76–77)

One should know that in this context, the duration [of the vowels] is merely that much; however, among the five consonants, a consonant (vyañjana) shall consist of half a mora (ardhamātra), while in some cases it may be one mora (ekamātra).
One should know it to be two moras (dvimātra) there, but never three moras (trimātrika).
There is a distinction regarding vowels that follow [another vowel]: it would consist of one *mātrā*. However, if there is a single consonant before it, it would consist of two *mātrās*.
That which has *ai*, *au*, or *ś* preceding it is said to consist of a mere atom (*aṇumātra*). 79–80.
Others say that a *mātrā* consists of a mere *truṭi*; there is no doubt that this is an excess of vowels.
A *mātrā* consists of four *aṇus*, while half of that would be a *truṭi*. This duration applies during the time of the Vedas, but it does not apply in the common language (*bhāṣā*).
For one with a firm voice, scholars require an excess of effort;
for one with a soft voice, it should be very slight, while for one with a medium voice, it should be moderate.
One should not exceed one's capacity, yet the subsequent recitation must necessarily be performed. 82–83.
One should not give [the Veda] to one who does not wish to listen; if one does, there is no doubt that hell [awaits].
When men abandon the Veda even after having studied it, they should be known as killers of an embryo (bhrūṇahā) and enter into a base womb.
Constant study of the Vedas, a habit of self-restraint, compassion, truthfulness, and discipline—
by these one attains purity and achieves the state of divinity. Thus ends the Kauṇḍinya Śikṣā, the Eighty-Six [Verses].
